say.text: A 2-year-old with known TOF has been crying hard for several minutes. He is now deeply blue, breathing fast and going limp.
You are the doctor on call. What do you do first?

choices.label: Place him in the knee-chest position
Give IV furosemide for the breathlessness
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Blood chooses between two exits: the narrowed RVOT or the aorta. Which resistance could you raise at the bedside, using only his legs?
Yes. Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance, so the blood is less keen to leave through the aorta. A spell needs a rapid, aggressive approach.
Spells can be set off by agitation, pain, anaemia, fever, hypovolaemia or peripheral vasodilatation, so crying fits the story.
Furosemide is tempting: a breathless, limp, blue child looks like heart failure. But this is a resistance problem, not a pump problem.
The measures used for a spell act on RV filling and systemic afterload, for example IV fluid boluses and IV phenylephrine. A diuretic empties the RV further.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the spell is about resistance and RV filling, not about congestion.

say.text: Intubation is tempting because he looks close to collapse and a rapid, aggressive approach is needed.
But the aggressive approach is made of simple levers: systemic vascular resistance, pulmonary vasodilation and RV filling.
Find the lever you can pull in seconds, without equipment.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause on this: the named measures are levers on resistance and filling, not airway control.

say.text: Knee-chest positioning is the hospital version of squatting.
What does it do?

choices.label: Cuts venous return to the right heart

say.text: Remember the balance: blood goes wherever the resistance is lower, RVOT or aorta. Squatting kinks the legs' vessels.

Right. Knee-chest increases systemic vascular resistance. If RVOT resistance is less than systemic resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic; raise systemic resistance and the balance tips that way.
Pulmonary resistance feels logical because the lungs are short of blood. And oxygen does cause pulmonary vasodilation.
But squatting is not the pulmonary lever. Knee-chest works on the other side of the balance: it increases systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one matters: oxygen is the pulmonary vasodilator, positioning is the systemic lever.

say.text: Less venous return sounds like unloading a struggling heart. Yet the fluid bolus given in a spell does the opposite: it improves RV filling.
Positioning works on resistance, not filling: it increases systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: filling is helped, not cut, in a spell.

say.text: You listen as the spell is at its worst. At clinic last week his harsh murmur was loud. Now it is barely audible.
How do you read this?

choices.label: The murmur has softened, as expected in a spell
It is better: the obstruction must be easing
Left heart failure is muffling the sounds

say.text: In the spell, where does most of the blood go: through the narrowed outflow, or around it?
Yes. In a spell the murmur decreases in intensity. Most blood shunts toward the aorta and bypasses the pulmonary bed.
Do not mix it up with the resting rule: the greater the obstruction, the more prominent the murmur.
A quieter murmur looks like less obstruction, and at rest a greater obstruction does give a more prominent murmur.
But a spell is a different state: the murmur decreases in intensity as blood bypasses the pulmonary bed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the reversed-mechanism trap: soft murmur in a spell means worse, not better.

say.text: Faint sounds and a limp child suggest failure, so this is a natural guess.
But the tetralogy explanation is simpler: during a spell the murmur decreases in intensity because most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the lungs.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: in a spell, think shunt, not pump failure.

say.text: Knee-chest and oxygen are under way. The registrar orders an IV fluid bolus for the blue, dry-looking child. A student protests that fluids worsen failure.
What is the bolus for?

choices.label: It should be withheld, as in heart failure

say.text: Yes. IV fluid boluses improve RV filling. Hypovolaemia is also one of the triggers of a spell.

Lowering systemic resistance would seem to help blood reach the lungs. But the spell measures push the other way: positioning increases systemic vascular resistance and phenylephrine increases systemic afterload.
Fluid has its own job: it improves RV filling.
Fluid restriction is the instinct from heart failure, and the student sounds careful. But a spell is not treated as failure.
Fluid boluses are part of the spell measures, to improve RV filling.
Spell still going. Which set matches the measures used in a tet spell?

choices.label: Knee-chest, oxygen, fluid bolus, phenylephrine, morphine for sedation
Furosemide, digoxin and fluid restriction, then reassess
Intubate and ventilate first, then give drugs once secured

say.text: Yes. Each pulls a lever: knee-chest raises systemic resistance, oxygen causes pulmonary vasodilation, fluids improve RV filling, phenylephrine increases systemic afterload.
IV beta-blockers decrease heart rate and aid RV filling further, and morphine can be given as a sedative.
This is the heart-failure bundle, tempting because the child is blue and breathless.
It pulls the wrong levers. The spell measures are fluid boluses for RV filling and phenylephrine for systemic afterload.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep this contrast: spell measures raise resistance and filling; failure drugs do neither.

say.text: Securing the airway first looks safe and the situation is urgent.
But the listed measures are knee-chest positioning, oxygen, IV fluid boluses, IV beta-blockers, IV phenylephrine and morphine as sedation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the spell measures are quick levers on resistance, vasodilation and filling.
